# Sum of Squares — Count Quadratic Contributions

## The identity to remember

$$
\sum_{k=1}^{n}k^2=\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}6
$$

**Every symbol explained:** n is the largest positive integer; k² is k multiplied by itself; Σ sums squares of all integers 1 through n.

**Substitute actual numbers:** For n=3, 1²+2²+3²=1+4+9=14. Right side: 3×4×7/6=14.

## Why it is true

Use the telescoping identity (k+1)³−k³=3k²+3k+1. Summing from k=1 to n, combine the known sums of k and 1 and solve for Σk².

## When to recognise it

This is a handy closed form for variance calculations, sum-of-square costs and nested loops whose inner work scales with k².

## Algorithm or number puzzle application

An outer loop doing i² work at iteration i for i=1..n has total Θ(n³), since the exact sum grows like n³/3.

## Assumptions and pitfalls

Use integer arithmetic carefully: multiplying n(n+1)(2n+1) before dividing may overflow a fixed-width type.

## Your turn

Compute 1²+2²+...+10² without ten multiplications.

**Memory rule:** Reconstruct the cancellation or counting argument before memorising the formula.
